idiom_name: SQLAlchemy ForeignKey + relationship(back_populates), or Django ForeignKey
implementation_notes: SQLAlchemy declares the column as the key (mapped_column(ForeignKey("customers.id"))) and the reference as relationship(back_populates="orders") on both sides; the Session identity map guarantees one object per row and lazy="select"/"joined"/"selectin" decides when the referenced row is fetched. Django's models.ForeignKey(Manufacturer, on_delete=models.CASCADE) is the declarative equivalent: it creates and indexes the column and emulates ON DELETE in Python, with db_constraint deciding whether a real constraint exists. Mapping rows by hand over DB-API cursors stays justified for reporting queries and for domain models that must not import an ORM.
code_sketch:
class Order(Base):
    __tablename__ = "orders"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    customer_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("customers.id"))
    customer: Mapped["Customer"] = relationship(back_populates="orders")

# session.get(Order, 7).customer -> resolved through the identity map
pitfalls: Touching order.customer inside a loop with lazy='select' is the N+1; selectinload/joinedload is the fix, and after the Session closes the same access raises DetachedInstanceError.
Django's on_delete is enforced in Python, not by the database: without db_constraint and a real constraint, raw SQL or another writer can still orphan rows.
Expired attributes re-query on attribute access at unpredictable times, so a session kept beyond one request produces surprise I/O and stale reads.
